source.title: Beyond Shallow Alignment: How Post-Training Methods Determine Refusal Circuits And Steering Robustness
source.authors: Hoang Cuong Nguyen; M. Dras; Usman Naseem

record.tranche_reason: It extracts the difference-in-means refusal direction and tests inference-time activation addition along it, measuring harmful-request ASR and MMLU accuracy. It does not perform the original all-layer, all-position projection ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper also measures refusal-direction geometry, circuit patching, and attack-class ASR. Results cited from other work are not recorded as this study's findings. Layer rankings used to select steering targets and qualitative examples are not separate rows. Steering values at intermediate strengths and other reported steering outcomes are omitted under the 60-row cap; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: Extracts the Arditi-style difference-in-means direction from 256 harmful/harmless pairs and adds or subtracts it (ActAdd) in SFT, Ra-SFT and ORPO checkpoints of three base models. It measures jailbreak ASR, XSTest over-refusal and MMLU, and compares direction geometry across training objectives. This bears on V1's addition and subtraction claims, on V7 and on V8 (thinking-mode Ra-SFT models). It does no full projection ablation and no weight edit.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the training objective, not just data, reshapes refusal-direction geometry, circuit structure, steerability and attack-class vulnerability, and that architecture independently matters. They find recognition-layer steering consistently beats execution-layer steering. They describe a trilemma: no offline objective jointly achieves distributed encoding, safety-utility separability and granular correctability. They also state DIM is only an approximation of refusal geometry, which may be a cone.
record.recipe_differences: Uses DIM from harmful/harmless prompt pairs and activation addition along the resulting refusal direction, but does not perform direction ablation or test removal at every layer and position. Steering is applied at selected layers; ITI uses per-head probes rather than the residual-stream DIM direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effects vary by model, training objective, target layer group (recognition versus execution), steering strength, and intervention method (ActAdd versus ITI). The study reports single evaluation runs for steering; target-layer hooks can also shift α=0 results.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-training method changes jailbreak ASR and over-refusal (ORPO lowest ASR; SFT highest over-refusal), with no direction measurement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety post-training objective changes refusal behaviour rates (a behavioural outcome, not direction mediation).

record.problems: The paper reports single steering evaluation runs, and explicitly notes that steering hooks can change baseline performance. It uses one model size per architecture, and reports 18/256 harmless prompts (7%) flipping from refusal to compliance across two matched Gemma ORPO runs. The authors caution that DIM only approximates refusal geometry. Some safety and utility measures use different evaluators (LlamaGuard-3 for ASR; heuristic string matching for ORR).
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was reached. Omitted Table 1 StrongREJECT ASR rows (all nine fine-tuned model/objective combinations); intermediate ActAdd strengths and additional MMLU values in Tables 8–11; Qwen3-8B Ra-SFT MMLU steering values; ITI steering outcomes and its generation-coherence failure examples; and attack-class ASR breakdowns in Figure 22. These were left out after retaining rows for each tested claim version, objective-related refusal/over-refusal results, key partial or capability-cost steering outcomes, and the reasoning-model condition.

untested.parts: No projection ablation of the direction at all layers and positions. Never tests induced refusal on harmless prompts as a refusal rate. No capability check under ablation.
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the direction. No adversarial training against ablation.
No comparison of single direction versus cone or affine; only discusses that DIM approximates the geometry.
No cross-language or cross-variant transfer test. Base-vs-post cosine is plotted but is not a transfer or intervention test.
Whether one removable direction exists after each objective is not tested by removal. Online preference methods and reasoning-plus-preference combinations are untested.
No ablation in reasoning models. Only two thinking-mode checkpoints (Gemma and Qwen Ra-SFT), addition only, single runs.

missing.what: Qwen3-8B SFT subtracting the direction at execution layers: ORR 63.6 to 44.0, ASR 31.2 to 39.6, MMLU stable. Removing the direction does unlock some harmful compliance here, unlike Gemma ORPO.
Gemma ORPO adding the direction: ASR 3.2 to 2.8, saturated at floor; MMLU 45-47.
Qwen3-8B Ra-SFT MMLU under addition: 64.5 to 59.0.

Cosine similarity of refusal directions, base vs post-trained and across objectives (Ra-SFT diverges; Gemma SFT-ORPO 0.8 to 0.72 late). Bootstrap direction stability >0.9 except Qwen post-trained early-mid layers (0.7-0.8).
Head-level ITI with per-head DIM probes. Gemma ORPO negative α raises ORR 30.8 to 33.2; Gemma SFT ASR flat; Llama generation collapses.

record.verdict_notes: Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B are fine-tuned from base models. Qwen3-8B Ra-SFT runs with thinking enabled; SFT and ORPO run with it disabled. Steering results are single runs, and the α=0 hook shifts baselines. Text and table disagree on some execution-layer reductions (5.8 vs 5.2pp; 4.6 vs 3.6pp); the table values are used. MMLU drops under addition were not counted as V1 capability failures, because V1's preservation claim concerns ablation and the paper does not separate induced refusal from incoherence. Llama ActAdd layers and ASR are not reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction, project it out of every layer and position, or test whether such removal eliminates refusal. Does not test whether adding the direction causes refusals on harmless prompts; steering results largely measure ASR on harmful prompts.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not directly compare single-direction, affine, or cone models of refusal. The discussion cites prior work on cone geometry and notes limitations of DIM.
Does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from the refusal decision.
Does not test transfer across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models.
Tests SFT, reasoning-augmented SFT, and ORPO on three architectures, but not other training methods, online preference methods, or interactions between reasoning and preference optimization.
Includes Qwen3-8B, described as a reasoning model, and reports steering results; does not establish generality to other reasoning models or reasoning configurations.

relation.reason: Its own steering results bear on V1, V7 and V8. The authors call the steering a probe of whether the direction mediates refusal.

tranche.reason: It uses Arditi's DIM direction (same 256 pairs) and activation addition, but measures WildJailbreak ASR (LlamaGuard), XSTest ORR and MMLU on self-trained SFT/Ra-SFT/ORPO checkpoints. It runs no ablation. The method differs, and the question (does the direction mediate refusal) is the same.

source_check.notes: Alpha scales the normalized direction r-hat (r divided by the mean activation norm, Eq. 1 and D.1). The text never gives the perturbation size relative to the residual stream, so nulls may be dose-limited. The ActAdd hook shifts alpha=0 baselines (Gemma Ra-SFT 36.0 vs 38.0; Qwen SFT 32.8 vs 31.2). All steering is single runs on a 250-prompt WildJailbreak subset. Llama ActAdd collapses MMLU at alpha=10 (SFT 35.5->0.0, Table 2) and no ASR is given, so check whether a row records this V1 capability cost. The prose and tables disagree: ORR 31.2 vs 31.6; 4.6/5.8pp vs 3.6/5.2pp; 28.2pp vs 27.2pp. Use the tables.

statements.correction: Optional addition: Qwen3-8B, ActAdd alpha=20: SFT recognition layers 32.8->5.6 (MMLU 59.0->30.0); Ra-SFT layers 31-35 32.4->30.8 (Table 10). SFT/Ra-SFT data: 16,000 Alpaca + 4,000 BeaverTails; ORPO: 11,179 BeaverTails preference prompts.
statements.problem: Numbers for this study are right (Llama 22-27, Qwen 22-30, Gemma ORPO late overshoot, 36.0->17.2, 43.2->35.2). Two caveats are left out. The Gemma Ra-SFT vs SFT comparison uses different layers (22-26 vs 27-31) and different alpha=0 baselines. In Qwen the objective contrast runs the other way. 'Matched data' is the authors' term, but ORPO used 11,179 BeaverTails paired prompts.

Correct for this study. Online preference methods are excluded, and no directional ablation is run under each objective. Subtraction (negative ActAdd) was run only in Gemma ORPO and Qwen SFT, to reduce over-refusal.

statements.correction: Ra-SFT steering: Gemma-2-9B recognition layers 36.0->17.2 (r28), Gemma execution layers 38.0->32.8, Qwen3-8B Ra-SFT (thinking mode) 32.4->30.8 (r44). Ra-SFT DIM magnitude profiles for Llama, Gemma, Qwen (r19-r21). Reasoning+preference combination untested.
statements.problem: Reasoning plus preference is indeed untested (Limitations). But 'one Ra-SFT steering row' understates this study. It reports Ra-SFT steering in two models, and Ra-SFT geometry in all three. Its Qwen3-8B Ra-SFT runs with thinking mode on.

statements.correction: arXiv:2609.03887, Gemma-2-9B Ra-SFT (emits <think> traces), ActAdd of the DIM direction at layers 22-26, alpha=20: WildJailbreak ASR 36.0->17.2 (250-prompt subset, LlamaGuard-3-8B judge, single run), MMLU 43.0->42.5.
statements.problem: Cites r28 but says nothing about this study in 'what' or 'conditions'. r28 measures jailbreak ASR on harmful prompts, not induced refusal on harmless prompts.
Correct. Could add that steering was at late layers 31-35, where recognition and execution coincide.

statements.correction: Same study, Qwen3-8B SFT (thinking off), recognition layers, alpha=20: ASR 32.8->5.6, MMLU 59.0->30.0 (Table 10).
statements.problem: Correct for this study, including the baseline shift from the hook. The measure also differs: here it is jailbreak ASR judged by LlamaGuard-3-8B, not a refusal rate. In the same study, Qwen3-8B SFT with thinking off does respond to addition.
